adjudications.evidence_summary: The implementation calls orders_for_user once for each listed user, and orders_for_user scans the complete order collection, directly establishing O(users × orders) work. The candidate's 40-user, 250-order probe reporting 10,000 user_id reads is consistent with this code path.
adjudications.scope_assessment: The failure is inherent in the supplied repository and list_users_with_order_counts implementation under its ordinary supported usage; it does not depend on hypothetical callers or infrastructure.
adjudications.materiality_assessment: The multiplicative scan can materially increase CPU consumption and response latency as both users and orders grow, making a production listing operation impractical on large datasets.

findings.claim: Listing users with order counts performs a full scan of all orders for every user, giving O(users × orders) work and causing CPU and response-time growth that can make the operation unusable on production-sized datasets.
evidence: evals/cases/case_08/src/users.py:15-16 loops over every user and invokes orders_for_user once per user.
evals/cases/case_08/src/users.py:9-10 implements each orders_for_user invocation by iterating through the entire _orders collection.
A runtime probe with 40 users and 250 instrumented orders observed exactly 10,000 user_id reads (40 × 250), while producing the correct aggregate count of 250 orders; the scoped test also passed.
